item.title: Gold price falls nearly 3% as CPI tops forecasts, lifting dollar and yields
item.description: Gold prices fell nearly 3% on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected US inflation data lifted the dollar and Treasury yields while reinforcing expectations of a
item.dc:creator: Mining.com
item.content:encoded: Gold prices fell nearly 3% on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected US inflation data lifted the dollar and Treasury yields while reinforcing expectations of a bigger interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve this year. Spot gold XAU= was down 2.8% at $4,021.36 per ounce by 11:33 a.m. ET (1635 GMT). US gold futures GCcv1 for December delivery fell 1.9% to $4,036.00 per ounce. “I think it’s a bit of a short-term negative for gold because the inflation numbers were running a little higher than expected,” said Edward Meir, an analyst at Marex. The US Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% last month after advancing 0.6% in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a 0.3% month-on-month rise. Bets on a 50-basis-point Fed rate hike in December started to build after the inflation print and comments by Fed governor Christopher Waller, who said he would support more aggressive action in the event of a too-hot Consumer Price Index report. The probability of a 25 bp hike is fully priced in, while the possibility of a 50 bp hike rose to 10.5% from 0% before the data, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool. The US dollar .DXY rose against a basket of other major currencies, and Treasury yields climbed. A stronger dollar makes gold more expensive for overseas buyers, while higher Treasury yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. “(Gold) continues to trade above the critical $4,000/oz mark,” Standard Chartered said in a note, adding “crude oil, inflation risks and equity markets continue to set the tone of trading for gold with a focus on rate hike expectations for the December Fed meeting.” Meanwhile, the Monetary Authority of Singapore said it would launch a vaulting service to hold bullion for foreign central banks and lower taxes on some companies in the gold market as it competes for a bigger slice of the precious metals trade. Spot silver XAG= fell 3.9% to $51.32 per ounce and palladium XPD= was down 2.0% at $1,021.22. (Reporting by Vedika Thorat and Anjana Anil in Bengaluru; Editing by Kirsten Donovan and Jonathan Ananda)

item.description: The meeting was postponed until January after Washington refused to take part, saying participation would imply support for the UN Human Rights Council.

item.content:encoded:

US skips UN human rights review, drawing criticism

The meeting was postponed until January after Washington refused to take part, saying participation would imply support for the UN Human Rights Council.

The empty seat of the US delegation, during the 60th session of the Human Rights Council, at the European headquarters of the United Nations in Geneva, Switzerland, on Sep 8, 2025. (Photo: AP/Salvatore Di Nolfi)

GENEVA: The Un ited States spurned a UN meeting on Tuesday (Nov 10) where its human rights record un der US President Donald Trump was due to be examined, drawing criticism from rights groups who say violations have surged to levels not seen in decades. Washington disengaged from the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Co un cil last year, citing an anti-Israel bias, and this is the second year in a row that it has skipped its own review - a process that even authoritarian state s take part in. The US left its seat on the stage of the UN meeting empty and the council decided to postpone the event until January. A US State Department spokesperson said participation would imply endorsement of the co un cil's work.

"This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own 'values' as it p us hes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, without responding to allegations about the US record. The 47-member co un cil has not directly criticised Washington's rights record but its appointed experts have, such as over migrant deportations. Washington said deportations wer e carried out in accordance with US immigration law.

QUESTIONS ON ABORTION AND DEATH PENALTY The Un iversal Periodic Review asks all 193 UN member states to submit a rights report every few years and these are review ed by other states , which provide non-binding recommendations. UN documents show co un tries had planned on Tuesday to raise issues such as abortion and the death penalty. US and international non-governmental organisations also sent nearly 200 UN submissions covering topics from migration to racial discrimination. “We've seen attacks on f un damental human rights and civil liberties un precedented in generations," Jamil Dakwar , of the American Civil Liberties Un ion , told reporters in Geneva. "Enough is enough." Fourteen co un tries are due to take part in the review process in Geneva this month. In Trump's first term in office, the US submitted its UPR report. Noor Abdalla, wife of pro-Palestinian student activist Mahmoud Khalil, who was held in immigration detention last year, is among campaigners pressing UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk to promptly hold a briefing on the US rights situation, even in Washington's absence. "When the most powerful government in the world is not held acco un table, they think that they can do whatever they want," Abdalla told reporters. However, diplomats were sceptical given that few states want to confront Washington. "The view is to leave the door open and hope they come back in two years," said a diplomat.

item.title: US CPI Exceeds Expectations Again, Waller's Warning Comes True! Wall Street Focuses on Whether December Rate Hike Will Be 25 or 50 Basis Points; "New Fed News Agency": Stop-and-Go Strategy Faces Test
item.description: The "New Federal Reserve Newsletter" pointed out that before the release of the CPI, Waller suggested the possibility of a 50-basis-point rate hike in December, and so far, no other Fed officials have publicly responded. In addition to a single 50-basis-point hike, the Fed may also choose to signal consecutive rate hikes in December and January. Wall Street generally believes that inflationary pressures remain stubborn, further strengthening the case for a rate hike in December, though a 50-basis-point increase is not a consensus. The market is concerned about whether the Fed will extend the tightening cycle.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: US inflation in October once again exceeded expectations, further raising market expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, with the possibility of a larger rate increase now being discussed. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) announced on Tuesday, November 10, that the October CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month, lower than the 0.6% increase in September but higher than economists’ forecasts of 0.3%. The core CPI rose 0.3% month-on-month, matching September’s increase and exceeding the market’s expectation of 0.2%. This marks the third consecutive month where overall CPI rose more than Wall Street predicted, and core CPI has also climbed 0.3% month-on-month for three straight months. Due to the failure to collect CPI data during the US federal government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS was unable to provide a year-on-year figure for October CPI. This report precisely meets the policy threshold previously outlined by Federal Reserve Governor Waller. Just hours before the CPI was published, Waller stated that if the core CPI for October increased by 0.3% or more month-on-month, he might support a 50 basis point rate hike at the Fed’s monetary policy meeting in December. With this criterion now met, the market’s bets on a 50 basis point rate hike in December have gained momentum. Nick Timiraos, a journalist nicknamed the “New Fed Whisperer,” pointed out that this inflation report is testing the Fed’s previous strategy of “spacing out rate hikes,” using staggered moves to leave room to monitor economic data. The choices facing policymakers are not only between a 25 or 50 basis point hike in December, but also whether to adjust the pace of subsequent actions, or even to signal back-to-back rate hikes in December and January of next year. Wall Street’s reaction is showing a common assessment: inflationary pressures remain stubborn, providing more justification for a December rate hike, though opinions differ on the size of the increase. Some believe that three consecutive months of core CPI climbing 0.3% makes it difficult for the Fed to ignore the inflation rebound; others feel that a 50-basis-point hike may be too aggressive and that 25 basis points is still the more realistic option. The market’s real concern is not just the decision at the next meeting but also whether the Fed may extend the tightening cycle as a result. “New Fed Whisperer”: Core prices strengthen across the board, Fed could signal back-to-back hikes In his analysis in The Wall Street Journal, Timiraos noted that the strong showing of October inflation is testing the Fed’s strategy of spreading out rate hikes across different meetings to allow time to observe economic data. He noted that Waller has raised the possibility that if the third month’s inflation data remains hot, a 50-basis-point rate hike in December could be on the table. However, no other Fed officials have publicly echoed this position as of yet. The Fed could also choose another way to address inflationary pressures: instead of a one-off 50-basis-point increase at a single meeting, it could signal consecutive rate hikes in December and January. According to Timiraos, this could be one way to adjust the policy pace. The last time the Fed raised rates by more than 25 basis points at once was back in 2022. On social media, Timiraos further broke down the details of core inflation, pointing out that core prices “strengthened broadly” in October. Specifically, core goods prices rose at a 1% annualized pace over the past six months, compared with just 0.1% in the previous period through June; core services prices excluding shelter rose 0.4% in October, about 4.9% annualized, while three- and six-month annualized increases stood at 5.5% and 3.2% respectively. He also pointed out that the unrounded month-on-month increase in core CPI for October was 0.296%, marking the third straight month at about 0.3%. The three-month annualized rate for core CPI climbed to 3.75%, compared with only 1.6% in July. This data shows that inflationary pressures are not just driven by overall energy price increases—core goods and services prices are also consistently strengthening. For the Fed, this makes it harder to treat inflation as a short-term shock and simply wait for price pressures to subside on their own. Waller raises 50-basis-point option, market begins to reassess policy strength Just hours before the CPI was released, Waller gave a hawkish speech while attending an event in London. He said the US economy was experiencing strong growth and a stable labor market, but inflation remained too high, requiring the Fed to “tighten policy sooner rather than later.” Waller had previously supported the Fed’s decision to keep rates unchanged at the last meeting, arguing that previous policy communications had already led financial markets to price in some degree of tightening. He believes policy adjustments do not have to be implemented in consecutive meetings, but prior guidance on rate hikes must eventually be delivered on, otherwise markets may lower expectations for further tightening, causing financial conditions to ease prematurely. Regarding the December meeting, Waller had already indicated before the CPI was published that if the October core CPI once again rose by around 0.3% month-on-month (as in the previous two months) or even higher, more forceful policy action might be needed. He explicitly raised the possibility of a 50-basis-point hike, and warned that if inflation remained high and price pressures broadened, raising rates by only 25 basis points could hurt the Fed’s credibility in fighting inflation. Ultimately, the October core CPI met this threshold. According to Reuters, after the data was announced, market expectations for a 25-basis-point rate hike in December were almost certain, and bets on a 50-basis-point hike rose to about 15% at one point. The two-year US Treasury yield surged, recording its largest single-day rise since early April 2025. However, Timiraos also cautioned that no other Fed official has publicly echoed Waller’s 50-basis-point position so far. Thus, the market’s discussion of a larger rate hike does not necessarily mean consensus within the Fed. Wall Street divided: Inflation pressures cannot be ignored, but 50 basis points is not a consensus After the inflation data was released, several Wall Street figures said the reasons for a December Fed rate hike had increased, but assessments of the scale and the persistence of inflation pressures varied. Omair Sharif, President of Inflation Insights, commented that the latest report “offers little to ease market concerns about persistent inflation risks” and does not dispel the Fed’s reasons for further hikes. He also estimated that the October core PCE price index might climb by 0.34%, representing an annualized increase of over 4%, higher than the previous month. While the Fed’s 2% policy target is based on headline PCE inflation, core PCE better reflects the underlying inflation trend. If this estimate is confirmed by subsequent data, it would further justify Fed tightening. James McCann, Senior Economist at Edward Jones, described this as another “disappointing inflation report,” reflecting that underlying price pressures may be building again. With US economic growth and the labor market both clearly accelerating this year, and core inflation showing signs of reacceleration, the Fed faces even greater policy pressure. McCann pointed out that the real worry is whether inflation is settling at a higher level. He argued the report at least solidifies the rationale for a 25-basis-point hike in December, while the bigger debate has become whether the Fed needs a 50-basis-point hike and more aggressive action. Peter Cardillo, Chief Market Economist at Spartan Capital Securities, also believes a December rate hike is virtually certain, with the suspense lying in whether it will be 25 or 50 basis points. He commented that Waller has effectively paved the way for a half-point hike, and the latest data shows inflation remains an issue. However, Cardillo also cautioned that circumstances could still change over the next 30 to 40 days. Should oil prices retreat and pass through to consumer prices, inflationary pressures may ease; but if oil rebounds, the inflation outlook could deteriorate again. Chris Zaccarelli, Chief Investment Officer at Northlight Asset Management, believes inflation above an ideal level further increases the likelihood of a December Fed hike. Still, despite market calls for a 50-basis-point hike, he expects the Fed will only lift rates by 25 basis points next month. Joe Saluzzi, Co-Head of Themis Trading, likewise noted that persistently high core inflation shows that price pressures have “stickiness” and that a 25-basis-point hike remains realistic, while 50 basis points may be too aggressive. He also warned that prolonged high rates and inflation will continue to pressure borrowing-dependent businesses, affecting profits and stock valuations. Skyler Weinand, Chief Investment Officer at Regan Capital, stated that the latest CPI paves the way for another Fed rate hike in December—the central bank cannot ignore the clear rebound in inflation data. He also pointed out that the latest jobs report showed robust employment gains in October as well as upward revisions to previous months’ data, providing the Fed with more room for further hikes. Labor market remains resilient, tightening policies may persist longer Besides inflation itself, the continued resilience of the US labor market also provides the Fed more leeway to prioritize combating inflation in its policy decisions. In his speech on Tuesday, Waller noted that US unemployment fell to 4.1% in October, with 165,000 new jobs added that month and a combined upward revision of 85,000 jobs over the prior two months. Although the average monthly jobs gains over the past six and twelve months is about 80,000, the overall labor market remains in a broadly balanced state, with no significant deterioration. This means the Fed, faced with persistently high inflation, need not worry about the impact of rate hikes on jobs as much as it would if the labor market were visibly weakening. Brian Jacobsen, Chief Economic Strategist at Annex Wealth Management, pointed out from a price transmission angle that three consecutive months of core CPI rising 0.3% month-on-month shows that the issue isn’t just high headline CPI, but that energy shocks may have begun to seep into core inflation. He also mentioned that Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee previously discussed how AI demand could be a new source of inflationary pressure for the Fed. As AI investment and infrastructure expansion rise, economic activity may crowd out resources in other areas and push up prices for some services. Jacobsen suggests the Fed may increasingly focus on the resource squeeze from AI demand and rising wage costs for skilled trades like plumbers and electricians. Jeff Schulze, Chief Investment Strategist at Franklin Templeton Institute, warned that the latest inflation data will serve as a headwind for risk assets. Investors are beginning to price in a 50-basis-point December hike and more afterward; rising short-term yields and a stronger US dollar could both suppress equity valuations. Karen Manna, Fixed Income Investment Strategist at Federated Hermes, also said the report strengthens the rationale for another Fed rate hike and further demands policymakers maintain vigilance. The real concern for investors is that if inflation remains high, the Fed may have to keep monetary policy restrictive for an extended period, well into 2027. Overall, the October CPI brings a December rate hike closer to market consensus, but the policy options facing the Fed are no longer just whether to raise rates. Waller’s 50-basis-point option, Timiraos’ comments on rate-hike spacing, and whether other officials will support speeding up the pace of tightening—all will be key market focuses going forward.

item.title: CPI Deals a Blow to US Bonds! 2-Year Yield Surges Over 20 Basis Points Intraday, Gold and Silver Plunge
item.description: After the release of the CPI, traders began to expect a lower likelihood of a 50 basis point rate hike in December; this year’s Federal Reserve voting member Logan stated that a faster pace of rate hikes may be needed this winter, with at least two more 25 basis point hikes required before pausing. Subsequently, the rise in U.S. Treasury yields continued to widen, with the 10-year yield climbing back above 5.0% and rising more than 10 basis points intraday; spot gold once fell over 3%, while spot silver at one point dropped more than 4%.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: In October, U.S. inflation once again exceeded market expectations, triggering a sell-off in U.S. Treasury bonds and a sharp rise in yields across the board. The strengthening U.S. dollar and heightened expectations for higher interest rates also put pressure on gold and silver. With Federal Reserve officials repeatedly sending hawkish signals, markets are not only increasingly betting on a rate hike in December but are also beginning to assess the possibility of a larger hike and further monetary policy tightening into next year. On Tuesday, U.S. Eastern Time, after the release of the U.S. CPI data, U.S. Treasuries were heavily sold, sending prices plunging and yields accelerating higher. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield expanded its gains following the CPI release and, after remarks by Federal Reserve official Lorie Logan, briefly broke above 5.01% during the U.S. stock market midday session, rising more than 10 basis points on the day. The 2-year Treasury yield, which is more sensitive to Fed policy expectations, climbed even more, surpassing 4.77% during midday and jumping more than 20 basis points on the day, on course for its biggest single-day surge since April last year. Precious metals markets also came under pressure. After the U.S. CPI release, gold extended its losses during the session. In the U.S. stock market midday, New York gold futures hit an intraday low of $4,020.8 per ounce, dropping nearly 2.3% on the day; spot gold fell below $4,014 per ounce, down nearly 3.1% intraday. The decline in silver was even more pronounced. Market data shows that at the day's lows in New York's midday, silver futures fell nearly 3% intraday, while spot silver plunged over 4%. CPI Inflation Continues to Beat Expectations for Months, Bond Market Reprices Fed Policy Path The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Tuesday that October CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month, higher than the market expectation of 0.3%, but slowed from 0.6% in September. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, also rose 0.3% month-on-month, surpassing expectations of 0.2% and matching September’s increase. This marks the third consecutive month of 0.3% gains for core CPI. Due to the U.S. federal government shutdown at the same time last year, which prevented data collection, the Bureau did not release year-on-year CPI data for October. Just hours before the CPI data was released, the market was already rattled by hawkish remarks from Fed Governor Christopher Waller. In a speech in London on Tuesday, Waller said that even if inflation improved in October, he would still be inclined to support a 25 basis point Fed rate hike in December. However, if core CPI reached 0.3% or higher for a third straight month, the Fed should consider a 50 basis point hike in December. He warned that raising rates by only 25 basis points could undermine the credibility of the Fed’s fight against inflation. The actual core CPI published hit Waller’s 0.3% threshold precisely. After the data release, markets quickly ramped up bets on a larger rate hike. Reuters reported that traders’ implied probability of a 50 basis point hike by the Fed in December spiked to about 13.6%, from near zero before the data was released; by contrast, a 25 basis point hike had already become the mainstream market expectation. According to Bloomberg, the inflation data triggered a sell-off in Treasuries, with short-term maturities bearing the brunt. Money markets also increased bets that the Fed will hike rates at least two more times by mid-2027, and began more clearly pricing in the possibility of a one-off 50 basis point hike in December. Lindsay Rosner, Head of Multi-Sector Fixed Income Investing at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said that if CPI remains robust, the Fed may usher in a more aggressive tightening cycle. Her view reflects market worries over persistently high inflation: even if a December hike is now the baseline expectation, future policy rates could still be more hawkish than previously anticipated. This Year’s FOMC Voter Logan: Faster Rate Hikes May Be Needed This Winter, Fed Needs at Least Two More 25 Basis Point Hikes Before a Pause Following the CPI release, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also sent further signals of policy tightening. Logan is a voting member of the FOMC this year. Speaking at an energy conference co-hosted by the Dallas Fed and the Kansas City Fed on Tuesday, she said that given current economic and inflation prospects, the Fed still needs to implement at least two additional 25 basis point hikes. Logan noted that the specific pace of hikes depends on the near-term economic and financial environment, and that the Fed might need to move faster this winter than it has this autumn. She stated, "It may be necessary this winter to act more quickly than the FOMC has so far this autumn." However, Logan is not advocating for continuous rate hikes. She said that after completing these two hikes, the Fed could pause to assess the economy and financial markets before deciding on further policy adjustments. She also emphasized that if inflation remains above target for an extended period, it could gradually become entrenched in business and household expectations, making timely action crucial. Logan’s comments signal that some Fed officials are discussing not just whether to hike rates in December, but also how to reach a moderately restrictive level more quickly. Her statements echoed Waller’s, further fueling market concerns about the Fed tightening policy even more over the coming months. U.S. Treasury Yields and Dollar Rise Together, Doubling Pressure on Gold and Silver Both U.S. Treasury yields and the dollar are strengthening, putting pressure on non-yielding precious metals. On one hand, higher bond yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing assets like gold and silver; on the other hand, a stronger dollar makes dollar-denominated precious metals more expensive for holders of other currencies. According to Reuters, after October inflation data came in higher than expected, gold prices fell noticeably as the market began evaluating the chances of the Fed taking a more aggressive rate-hiking stance. Gold is especially sensitive to changes in interest rate expectations, and if the market further raises its outlook for policy rates, precious metals could continue to face pressure in the short term. However, the future path for gold and silver will not depend solely on Fed policy. Movements in the dollar, geopolitical risks, energy prices, and investors’ outlook on the economy can all affect demand for precious metals. The key market shift currently is that both the inflation data and hawkish comments from Fed officials have reinforced expectations for higher rates, forcing a reset in precious metals trades that previously benefited from rate-cut expectations.

item.title: Alleged spy plot targeting CEO raises questions about Nvidia's future
item.description: Investigations into whether Nvidia's CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort" are raising questions about the future of the chipmaker, which became one of the world's most valuable ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Alleged spy plot targeting CEO raises questions about Nvidia's future

Alleged spy plot targeting CEO raises questions about Nvidia's future Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia since he co-founded it more than 30 years ago

The company now faces potential damage to its reputation and stock price, uncertainty over a possible successor and new scrutiny from shareholders and elected officials (Photo: Reuters)

AP San Francisco 5 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 7:53 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Investigations into whether Nvidia's CEO was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort" are raising questions about the future of the chipmaker, which became one of the world's most valuable companies by providing technology that powered the artificial intelligence boom. Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia since he co-founded it more than 30 years ago. The company now faces potential damage to its reputation and stock price, uncertainty over a possible successor and new scrutiny from shareholders and elected officials. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. But Trump said he spoke with the executive and believes Huang "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."   With a valuation of more than USD 4 trillion, the company has outsized importance as a Wall Street behemoth and provider of chips relied upon by AI developers. Law enforcement and members of Congress, as well as Nvidia's board and shareholders, are all asking questions about the affair. The company's shares dropped more than 4 per cent Monday and continued sinking Tuesday morning.

Nvidia's identity has been tied to Huang himself Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the centre of decision-making. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace Huang is unclear. "The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options. Jensen is Nvidia," said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. "And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed and they have no successors, that's a terrible outcome."   Replacing Huang would be challenging in part because his public profile is so closely associated with Nvidia.

Also Read

Nvidia investigates alleged spy plot involving its CEO: What we know

Wall St slips as hot inflation data fuels rate-hike jitters; Nvidia down 4%

Nvidia CEO's spy affair sparks shock, disbelief in his birthplace Taiwan

Jensen Huang's fortune takes $7.4 billion hit as Nvidia probes affair

Nvidia CEO's alleged China spy link promised investors access to AI chips

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor of leadership at the Yale School of Management, compared Huang's relationship with Nvidia to Steve Jobs' role at Apple. Down to Huang's signature leather jacket, like Jobs' turtleneck, Nvidia is "symbolically and substantively, inextricably intertwined around his personal aura."   Other tech executives, such as Oracle's Larry Ellison and Microsoft's Bill Gates, have also been deeply intertwined with the success of their companies, making it hard to separate them. But in those cases, the companies "can still be successful long after the original founders have taken on a lesser role," said Dan Morgan, vice president and senior portfolio manager at investment firm Synovus Trust.

If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress. Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are "lots of other great leaders" within the company, said Bob O'Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research. "I think it's important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen," O'Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.

Huang had the Midas touch, but his reputation is at risk During his 33-year tenure at the helm of Nvidia, Huang built a reputation as a trusted business leader and an established voice within the technology world. He cultivated close relationships with other tech executives, as well as with Trump, helping to persuade him to take a lighter touch on regulating AI. "Everybody wanted to have that Midas touch of his when it comes to technology," O'Donnell said. But the scandal is a growing liability for Huang and Nvidia at a delicate time for the AI industry after the midterm elections in the US ushered in a wave of Democrats promising tougher regulation. Top Democrats Senator Mark Warner and Representative Hakeem Jeffries said Monday they are interested in investigating further.

A shareholder on Monday sued Nvidia and Huang, accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses to media reports about Huang's affair with the purported Chinese spy. The complaint filed in a California court says the company misled investors about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who news reports said is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and the national security implications. The New York Times identified her as a business executive and Chinese citizen. Sonnenfeld said he places the odds that Huang stays on as CEO at roughly 50-50, but those odds are "slipping by the moment."   "He has lost the confidence and trust of his key constituents, his board, his employees," said Sonnenfeld, who is also founder and president of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute. "And every employee knows that if anybody else had done this, they would have been fired long ago."   Some experts are more confident in the company's stability going forward. Morgan, of Synovus Trust, said that if Huang is required to step down to a lesser role at Nvidia following the company's investigation, he is "still confident that the company will continue to maintain its lead in the GPU AI chip market."   But at the same time, the affair "sounds more like a made-for-TV melodrama than a real story," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.description: Representative-elect LaKesha Womack, a community organiser who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-know North Carolina Republican on her shoestring USD 56,000 campaign budget, said ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Dreams, desks and selfies: New US lawmakers learn their way around

Dreams, desks and selfies: New US lawmakers learn their way around More than 100 newly elected lawmakers have arrived in Washington for orientation ahead of taking office on January 3

The US Capitol in Washington | Image: Bloomberg

AP Washington 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 7:52 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Representative-elect LaKesha Womack, a community organiser who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-know North Carolina Republican on her shoestring $56,000 campaign budget, said she's excited to arrive in Washington and show what's possible. Representative-elect Brian Poindexter said his win over incumbent GOP Representative Max Miller ensures Ohio remains a very swing state. And Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot in New Jersey who said she's spent her whole life "trying to find the biggest, hardest problem to throw myself at," was ready to give Congress a try. "There's always the unknown."   They were among more than 100 newly elected members of Congress arriving in Washington this week for the start of freshmen orientation -- the crush of new Democrats, many bringing a new sense of urgency after the party's sweep of the midterm elections, and the slim new class of freshmen Republicans.

"People were just looking for somebody who's going to listen to them," said Womack, who said she won by simply showing up and talking with voters. "I'm a single mom and so I know what it's like to have to live on a budget and figure out how am I going to feed my family," she said. "And that's what people want to fight for them in Washington right now."   New-member orientation creates an unusual mash-up on Capitol Hill, as the newcomers are arriving and the exiting lawmakers begin to clear out, all in preparation for the peaceful transfer of power on January 3, when lawmakers are sworn in and the new Congress begins.

Also Read

US midterm results may ease India's oil import bill, but tariff risks stay premium

Democrat control of Congress may bring limited gains for India-US ties premium

Exim matters: US verdict lifts hopes; mkts celebrate, but traders cautious premium

Russia hopes US poll shake-up won't shift Trump's negotiations on Ukraine

SpaceX director Donald Harrison resigns from board a day after US election

This week's orientation includes training sessions and ritzy receptions for the newcomers, and for the defeated or retirees it's the start of figuring out what's next. Briefing rooms are filled with information about office set up, payroll and benefits, and there's a room to take officials portraits. It's also the time for the House and Senate to hold internal party elections for their new leaders, ahead of a public vote in January for the speaker of the House. "I'm looking forward to learning as much as I can and being the best representative I can be for my district," said Poindexter as he arrived at the nearby Navy Yard hotel where lawmakers are temporarily housed.

Selfies, besties and tough votes ahead The Capitol was a changed place as the members-elect started meeting up with their colleagues and getting to know their way around the place. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan was swarmed by young people in the Capitol basement, taking pictures with the progressive star who is also the first Muslim in the Senate. Texas Senator-elect James Talarico paid a visit to the outgoing Texas Republican Senator John Cornyn, who lost his own primary for reelection when President Donald Trump backed his rival, Ken Paxton, who was defeated. "I'm so grateful for his advice and his guidance as I try to fill his big shoes," Talarico said of Cornyn as he walked through the Senate between orientation events. He said he wants to meet with Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas as well.

And Senator-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois snapped a photo with new Democratic senators-elect including Talarico, El-Sayed, Annie Andrews, Roy Cooper, Peggy Flanagan, Josh Turek and others. "First Freshmen Senator selfie! Couldn't ask for a better team," she posted as the caption. Among them was former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted, a Trump-backed favourite, for a comeback. Brown was in the Senate for 18 years before he lost two years ago to GOP Senator Bernie Moreno, but he still joined his freshmen colleagues for their orientation. "I've actually learned some things," said Brown, who was celebrating his 74th birthday on Monday. "I've gotten to know my colleagues."

Leadership elections test the new members One of the first decisions the incoming lawmakers will make happens even before they're sworn into office, as they huddle with their parties in private meetings to choose House and Senate leadership. Congressional offices are being bombarded with phone calls and social media messages pushing Democrats to dump their current choices -- House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer -- in favour of a fresh start. Jeffries scoffed when questioned Monday if he had support-- the typically low-key leader flashing confidence he would have the votes. He is on track to make history as the nation's first Black American to become speaker of the House.

Progressive lawmakers, in particular, are agitating for change reflective of voters' sweeping turnout for Democrats, especially in the Senate. Senator-elect Chris Pappas, Democrat-New Hampshire -- who was darting back and forth between his day job as an outgoing member of the House and his new one as an incoming senator -- said their class is "a new generation of leadership that wants to do things differently and shake up Washington."   He said he wants to meet with Schumer and will later decide who he will support, if anyone challenges him. Republicans will also choose their new leaders after House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to step aside following the party's election defeat. Tuesday's closed-door race between the No. 2 Republican Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Ohio Representative Jim Jordan is a repeat of the contest in 2023, before Johnson rose to power.

Representative Richard Hudson, the House GOP campaign chairman who lost his own reelection bid in North Carolina, hesitated to assess the outcome. Besides, he said, he doesn't have a vote in the matter -- the exiting lawmakers are blocked from the GOP meeting. A diverse new class arrives As the week began, the House Chaplain Margaret Kibben opened Monday's session with a prayer, "some of us enjoying victories and others enduring disheartening defeats."   On the Democratic side, the new Congress will see many milestones -- Flanagan will be the first Native American female US senator, Pappas the first gay male senator, and more. Representative Suzan DelBene, the House Democrats campaign chief, called the party's candidates "all very unique."   "We had firefighters, ministers, mayors, veterans, teachers, farmers, prosecutors, union leaders, law enforcement, doctors, journalists and even a Grammy-award winning musician," she said earlier.

"They understand that their job title is representative, not rubber stamp."   Johnson, the outgoing speaker, hosted a reception in the Capitol's stately Statuary Hall for the House Republicans, whose shrinking numbers left the party lopsided, their minority made up of mostly white men.

item.title: Eisenkot targets Netanyahu-era policies as new Israeli parliament convenes
item.description: Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel's longest-serving prime minister ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Eisenkot targets Netanyahu-era policies as new Israeli parliament convenes

Eisenkot targets Netanyahu-era policies as new Israeli parliament convenes Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel's longest-serving prime minister

Gadi Eisenkot | Image: Reuters

AP Tel Aviv 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 7:51 AM IST

Listen to This Article

Gadi Eisenkot, the politician tasked with forming a new Israeli government, pledged on Tuesday to reverse many of Benjamin Netanyahu's policies as the new parliament was sworn in. The pledge sets the stage for a consequential month of legislative action and coalition negotiations. Eisenkot, a former military chief, has up to six weeks to form a government that would end the tenure of Israel's longest-serving prime minister. While it remains unclear whether Eisenkot will be able to forge a coalition government, the new Knesset can enact legislation in the meantime. Netanyahu's opponents now control a solid majority in parliament. Eisenkot's bloc introduced a series of bills at the start of the legislative session that target Netanyahu and his policies. They include launching an official government-led inquiry into Hamas' October 7, 2023, attacks, setting term limits on the position of prime minister and overturning changes the outgoing Netanyahu-led government made to limit the powers of the judiciary. It was not immediately clear how quickly or far those bills would advance in the weeks ahead.

Competing calls for unity The former general, who campaigned as a no-nonsense straight shooter, reiterated on Tuesday that his goal was a government that all Israelis could trust, not one that represents only certain factions. Also Read

PepsiCo to cut over 1,000 jobs amid sluggish sales in North American market

Netanyahu calls Trump daily to resume Iran war as US weighs ending conflict

Eisenkot gets first chance to form Israeli govt after tight election

Is Anthropic's mega IPO at risk over its $1.5 trillion valuation?

Trump says US will end $4 billion annual military aid to Israel by December

"We will act for all citizens of Israel, those who voted for us and those who did not, out of deep commitment," Eisenkot said ahead of the Knesset swearing-in ceremony. Netanyahu has sought to undermine the certified election results after his bloc fell short of a majority. He has repeated unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties "stole" the elections. In a speech following Tuesday's ceremony, Netanyahu attacked opposition leaders who have signalled a willingness to partner with Arab parties to form a government. Eisenkot has left that possibility open if the parties meet several conditions, including accepting Israel's identity as a Jewish state and declaring Hamas a terrorist group.

"I ask you: are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" Netanyahu said. Eisenkot called the speech "divisive" and "hate-filled." Netanyahu's opponents already have a legislative agenda Eisenkot's bloc also triggered a process on Tuesday to install a new parliamentary speaker as they kicked off work on their legislative agenda. A majority of members submitted signatures calling for the ousting of the current Netanyahu-backed speaker, Amir Ohana, the first step toward a vote on his replacement. The vote can take place even before a coalition government is in place. The Knesset speaker is a powerful position. The speaker determines what bills the Knesset will take up, meaning one picked from among the Eisenkot-led opposition parties could propel their legislative agenda forward.

The opposition nominated Matan Kahana, a senior member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, for the job. A vote to appoint him speaker could come as early as this week. Netanyahu as caretaker The swearing-in of the new Knesset ushered in an unusual transitional period in Israeli politics -- Netanyahu and his Cabinet remain in power, while the new lawmakers can introduce legislation. Meanwhile, Eisenkot will meet with party leaders as he works to build a coalition that would likely make him prime minister. If he fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to give Netanyahu the next opportunity to form a government. As caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu faces court-imposed limits on his powers. But he can still pursue appointments and could try to block new legislation. He retains full authority over national security, including the military.

Netanyahu has argued that Jewish-led parties should form a unity government to counter the threat of an Iranian attack. He renewed that call Tuesday, urging them to "set aside all other considerations," and said Israel should work to topple the Iranian government. A governing coalition without Netanyahu could leave him politically vulnerable as he faces an ongoing corruption trial and possible findings of security failures in the lead-up to the October 7 attacks.

MADRID, Nov 10 : Spain's government has demanded that TikTok suspend its operations in Spain until it eliminates child sexual abuse material, it said on Tuesday, after a media report documented 1,183 explicit posts on the platform with millions of views. Youth Minister Sira Rego, whose ministry cannot singlehandedly ban the platform in Spain, has appealed to prosecutors and the Data Protection Agency to take action against the social media company, according to a statement by the ministry. "Social media cannot be lawless territory," Rego said. The request comes months after Sanchez's government requested a probe into X, Meta and TikTok for allegedly spreading AI-generated child sexual abuse material, as European regulators intensify scrutiny of big tech over harmful and illegal content.

The organisation published a follow-up story on Tuesday evening stating that TikTok had restricted two of the search terms that Maldita.es's investigation identified as pathways to child sexual abuse content for users in Spain, but that searches from other European countries still led to the same content.

NEW YORK, Nov 10 : US electricity consumption will rise to record highs in 2026 and 2027 due to power-hungry AI data centers and electrification, the US Energy Information Administration said in its Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) on Tuesday. The EIA projected that power demand will rise from a record 4,216 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2025 to 4,306 billion kWh in 2026 and 4,370 billion kWh in 2027. If correct, 2026 would be the third year in a row of record demand. Demand is surging largely due to data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence. Homes and businesses have also been relying more on electricity and less on fossil fuels for heat and transportation. The EIA forecast that power sales in 2026 will rise to 1,546 billion kWh for residential consumers, 1,557 billion kWh for commercial customers and 1,061 billion kWh for industrial customers.

The all-time highs stand at 1,519 billion kWh for residential consumers and 1,503 billion kWh for commercial customers in 2025 and 1,064 billion kWh for industrial customers in 2000. As renewable output rises, the EIA said the share of power generation from coal will slide from 17 per cent in 2025 to 15 per cent in 2026 and 2027, while the share of natural gas in 2026 will hold steady from 2025 at 40 per cent, then ease to 39 per cent in 2027. The percentage of renewable generation will rise from around 24 per cent in 2025 to 25 per cent in 2026 and 28 per cent in 2027, while nuclear power's share will hold at 18 per cent in 2026 and 2027, the same as in 2025, according to the outlook. The EIA projected that gas sales in 2026 would slide to 12.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) for residential consumers and 9.4 bcfd for commercial customers, but rise to 23.8 bcfd for industrial customers and 37.4 bcfd for power generation. Those figures compare with all-time highs of 14.3 bcfd in 1996 for residential consumers, 9.9 bcfd in 2025 for commercial customers, 23.8 bcfd in 1973 for industrial customers, and 36.8 bcfd in 2024 for power generation.

Source: Reuters

item.title: NVIDIA Stocks Slide 4.43% as Report Alleges $7.5 Billion in Chips Reached China
item.description: NVDA shares fell 4.43% to $170.75 as of 9:53 a.m. ET in regular trading on November 10, after The Information reported that Jensen Huang's personal relationship with a businesswoman alleged to work ...
item.content:encoded:
News / GuruFocus / NVIDIA Stocks Slide 4.43% as Report Alleges $7.5 Billion in Chips Reached China

NVIDIA Stocks Slide 4.43% as Report Alleges $7.5 Billion in Chips Reached China 1 min read

NVDA NVIDIA NVDA shares fell 4.43% to $170.75 as of 9:53 a.m. ET in regular trading on November 10, after The Information reported that Jensen Huang's personal relationship with a businesswoman alleged to work for Beijing helped move at least $7.5 billion of its chips to Chinese firms. That stacks on Monday's 4.27% drop. Reuters, which carried the report, said it could not independently verify the claims. The report describes a web of companies in China and Singapore, centered on Shanghai Century Litong, that won preferred cloud-partner status within months of its June 2023 founding. When orders for export-restricted chips stalled, roughly 240,000 H100, H200 and A100 units allegedly reached China. Some of that capacity reportedly served Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese AI labs. The company's board said a committee of independent directors with outside counsel is running the review. The board added that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

From the November 6 close of $186.64, the two-day slide is 8.51%, roughly $383 billion of market value on about 24.1 billion shares. The GuruFocus profile is lopsided: GF Score 92/100, Profitability 10/10, Financial Strength 9/10 and Momentum 10/10, but GF Value Rank only 2/10. At $170.75 the shares trade 60.10% below the $427.93 GF Value, yet GuruFocus itself tags the setup "Possible Value Trap, Think Twice." The model gap alone is no bargain signal. The next hard test is the November 17 third-quarter report, where any export-control questions would surface in guidance or disclosures.

Defiant Hegseth blasts impeachment effort ahead of House vote

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth also thanked US President Donald Trump for his support as lawmakers prepared to vote on eight articles of impeachment against him.

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth holds a press briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, DC, on Nov 10, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein)

FAST

WASHINGTON: Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday (Nov 10) blasted efforts to impeach him as a farce that would embolden US adversaries, as he lashed out at his political opponents in Congress and the media in an unapologetic defence of his record. Striking a defiant tone at a Pentagon news briefing, Hegseth thanked US President Donald Trump for his continued support as the House of Representatives scheduled a procedural vote for late Tuesday that will test support for his impeachment. Hegseth said past impeachments of Trump had ultimately failed, and added: "Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House. Now they're trying a third time. This time against a member of his cabinet." US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment against H egseth on Monday. Massie said in a post on X that if the House of Representatives can overcome Tuesday's procedural effort, "we will proceed to a real debate and vote on the Articles of Impeachment".

Congressional sources say the resolution may have the votes to pass even with Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on Jan 3. Conviction appears unlikely in the Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats. Hegseth is accused of various abuses of power in office, including issuing orders to go to war with Iran without an imminent threat or approval from Congress. Voter anger over the Iran war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week's midterm elections . A new Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday found a majority of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran.

US Representative Thomas Massie holds a press conference about his resolution to impeach Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, on Nov 9, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein)

Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned the war. Hegseth declined to be drawn into responding to Vance, but defended the conflict, calling Trump courageous and saying Iran's military has been left in ruins. "History will judge the Iran war quite differently than the conventional wisdom right now," he said. Hegseth cited US Secretary of State Marco Rubio as saying of the war: "It's not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary, and that's certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking." Trump repeated his backing of Hegseth in a post on his Truth Social platform just after the Pentagon briefing ended. "Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!" he wrote. A polarising figure in American politics, Hegseth would be the first US defense secretary to be impeached. The last time any civilian leader of the US military was impeached was in 1876, when William Belknap held the title "secretary of war". Hegseth, a former Fox News host, calls himself secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and "woke" when he took office last year. But even some Republicans say his strained relations with Congress are becoming a political liability as the administration seeks a US$1.5 trillion defense spending package. In a possible nod to the spending requests, Hegseth said Republicans should use their final weeks in control of Congress to deliver wins for the American people instead of pursuing his impeachment. If he's still around next year, Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, including his firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other top military officers.

Related:

Trump vows comeback as bitter showdown with Congress looms

Trump says Hegseth doing 'a very good job' as questions swirl about his future

Source: Reuters/fs

Nov 10 : Anthropic said on Tuesday it was bringing its Claude assistant to video conference platform Google Meet, as the company pushes to integrate AI deeper into everyday office work. Earlier in the day, Anthropic launched a roadshow for its highly anticipated US initial public offering, with plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion at a $1.02 trillion valuation. The offering will test investors' appetite for the AI boom and Anthropic's massive spending plans. Called Claude Meetings, the new feature will let users add Claude to video calls as a visible participant. Anthropic said Claude would be able to follow the conversation and turn discussions into work in real time, while also drafting plans, creating timelines and answering questions in the call's chat. The feature is designed to shift AI's role in meetings from simply recording or summarizing conversations to doing the work that follows from them while the discussion is still taking place, Anthropic said.

The rollout is part of a broader push by Anthropic to make Claude an active participant in knowledge work. The company said it was also introducing Claude Whiteboards, which lets teams turn discussions into timelines and action plans, as well as Claude Sheets and Claude Data.

Nov 10 : IBM said on Tuesday that it was ending US visa and green card sponsorship for a majority of roles in IBM Consulting, which employs more than 150,000 people. The move comes amid tight scrutiny of foreign tech hiring by Donald Trump's administration. Last month, it suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several major outsourcers, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, from the Permanent Labor Certification process — a key step toward green cards for foreign workers. IBM Consulting has used US high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages, but participation has been declining for years, a company spokesperson told Reuters. It opted to end sponsorship for most such roles as skill availability and client needs have evolved, the spokesperson added.

FAST

WASHINGTON, Nov 10 : Alphabet's Google has agreed to additional privacy protections in the acquisition of employee data from defunct Spirit Airlines, a union representing employees said Tuesday. The agreement clears the way next week for approval of Google's $10 million deal to acquire Spirit data to train AI models. The union said it had won a more rigorous de-identification process than previously planned and added significant employee data will be excluded from the sale, including health and medical information. As part of Spirit's closure and asset liquidation, Google won an auction in August for data from emails, spreadsheets and calendars, as well as for marketing, productivity and operations. Spirit Airlines halted operations in May. A bankruptcy judge is now set to approve the deal next week.

The Association of Flight Attendants-CWA said the de-identified data will also be reviewed by an independent verification agent chosen in consultation with unions, and Google is prohibited from attempting to re-identify the data and is required to process it in a secure environment and treat it as confidential. A group of about 120 lawmakers raised concerns last month about the data sale. Last month, a privacy ombudsman recommended a US bankruptcy judge approve the deal after excluding passenger personal information from 97 million Spirit customers. The lawmakers, led by Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and Representative Steven Horsford, a Nevada Democrat, said the sale would include 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages and other employee records. Spirit Airlines said it was pleased to have reached a resolution with labor unions as it continueed to maximize value for its creditors. "We are grateful for the collaboration of Google, the consumer privacy ombudsman, our labor unions, and other key stakeholders who are engaging with us constructively on this sale," a spokesperson said. Google, which did not immediately comment Tuesday, said last month it did not want to acquire personal information. "We are not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit. The information will either be completely excluded or will be de-identified by an independent third party before Google receives any data," Google said last month.

Source: Reuters

item.title: Nvidia, CEO Huang sued over disclosures related to suspected Chinese spy
item.description: Nvidia and Chief Executive Jensen Huang were sued on Monday in a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang’s ties with a suspected Chinese spy.
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: Nvidia and Chief Executive Jensen Huang were sued on Monday in a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang’s ties with a suspected Chinese spy. According to a complaint filed in federal court in San Jose, California, the defendants misled shareholders about Huang’s alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him, and did not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that threatened Nvidia’s reputation and business prospects. The New York Times reported last month about the alleged relationship, and that U.S. authorities had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Jensen Huang told Nvidia’s employees he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the alleged relationship. He co-founded Nvidia, and has led the Santa Clara, California-based company as it became the world’s most valuable chipmaker and made him one of the world’s most prominent symbols of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia announced a probe into the matter on Sunday. Its shares closed down 4.3 per cent on Monday, reducing Nvidia’s market capitalization by approximately US$190 billion. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after the U.S. stock market closed. It is common for shareholders to sue companies after unexpected share price declines. Nvidia shareholders led by Mark Kistenmacher are seeking unspecified damages from the defendants. (Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York; Editing by Matthew Lewis)

item.title: Democrats Need to Make Jobs Central to Economic Policy
item.description: When it comes to the economy, newly elected Democrats have an intimidating to-do list. Voters were clear that they are struggling to afford their life, so the party needs to address deeply entrenched problems in markets for health insurance, housing, utilities, and elder and childcare. And in order to do any of that, Congress has to get the fiscal balance sheet in order and reform the tax code.
item.dc:creator: Kathryn Anne Edwards

item.title: US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review
item.description: The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review

US set to become first country to fully shun UN Human Rights Council review Trump administration declines to participate in the UN Human Rights Council's Universal Periodic Review, which examines the rights records of all 193 member states every four to five years

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago | Image: Bloomberg

AP Geneva 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 2:47 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The United States is set to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the UN's top rights body since it was created two decades ago. The Trump administration last year pulled the US out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-US and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes. Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all UN member states including the US, which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific - which the administration has said are designed to protect US workers and help keep the country safe.

The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 UN member states - generally about every four to five years - as part of a process known as the universal periodic review. The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the US government might change its mind. Also Read

Bangladesh's troubled history and questions about its political future

US visa curbs: Will Indian IT firms shift more technology work offshore?

Meet Nithya Raman, the India-born politician who won LA mayoral race

US AI data centres turn to retired jet engines to meet power demand

Private jet carrying 9 crashes near Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida

It did not. "(W)e give no credibility to the agency," a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. "This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own values' as it pushes anti-American rhetoric," the spokesperson said, alleging the council's "persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators."   The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations - which at times can include a dozen officials or more - make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies. Critics of the US snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries - many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors - to follow suit. Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: "The administration is saying to the world, we don't care about whether you would review us or not, we're going to continue to violate human rights unabashed'."   "And we are saying: No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable'," he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the US rights record.

He said the ACLU and allies have called on the UN human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year. Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the US walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system. "If the predominant global power - which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms - doesn't show up and doesn't even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Blast at steel plant kills 16 in Turkey
item.description: Another 13 people were injured following the blast, and 10 others are still waiting to be rescued.
item.dc:creator: Marina Meireles
item.content:encoded:
Blast at steel plant kills 16 in Turkey

Marina Meireles | November 9, 2026 | 1:01 pm News   Europe   Iron Ore

Stock image.

A blast at a steel and iron plant in western Turkey killed 16 people on Nov. 9, with search and rescue operations still ongoing to reach 10 people still trapped under the rubble, President Tayyip Erdogan said.

The explosion happened around noon local time, at the Habas Demir Celik facility in the Aliaga district of Turkey’s Izmir province, where iron and steel are processed.

The incident occured when a ceiling crane snapped and fell into an arc furnace during the molten steel casting process.

13 people were injured, and 2 were in serious condition, Bloomberg reported. The victims were transported to different hospitals in the region.

The government said the incident is under investigation.

(With files from Reuters and Bloomberg)

item.title: Copper price bounces after worst week since March amid scramble for metal in China
item.description: The Yangshan premium for copper shipped into China climbed to a record $230 a tonne on Monday, spot premiums in Shanghai have tripled in two weeks, and deliverable stocks on the SHFE would cover less than a day of Chinese consumption.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price bounces after worst week since March amid scramble for metal in China

Staff Writer | November 9, 2026 | 12:39 pm Markets   China   United States   Copper

Copper cathode production in electrowinning plant. ( Stock image by Jorge. )

Copper prices rebounded on Monday, recovering part of last week’s steep losses as risk appetite steadied, the dollar slipped and tight physical supply in China came back into focus.

Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, was trading at $6.3550 a pound ($14,010 a tonne) late morning in New York, up 1.9% on the day and roughly 13% higher so far in 2026.

On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper rose 0.9% to $13,890 a tonne by mid-afternoon in London, having lost 2.7% last week in its steepest weekly decline since March. In Shanghai the most-traded contract gained 0.5% to 107,430 yuan ($16,096) a tonne.

China squeeze

“Copper is recovering as risk sentiment stabilises and tight physical supply in China returns to focus,” ING commodities strategist Ewa Manthey told Reuters, adding that the rise in spot premiums shows metal remains difficult to secure.

The Yangshan copper premium, which reflects demand for metal imported into the top consumer, rose to a record $230 a tonne on Monday. Copper stocks in Shanghai Futures Exchange-monitored warehouses fell more than 24% last week to 33,848 tonnes, the lowest in almost three years, according to John Gross of The Copper Journal . That would cover China’s copper consumption for less than a day.

Bloomberg reports the Singapore-based trader Trafigura, one of the biggest in the copper market, has over the past two weeks approached several producers and traders in Asia seeking to buy large volumes over November and December, and has been willing to outbid rivals to secure cargoes.

Spot premiums in Shanghai have tripled over the past two weeks to a record 2,615 yuan ($392) a tonne, according to Shanghai Metals Market, while premiums for imported copper tracked by Fastmarkets have jumped more than 40% to $195–210 a tonne, the highest in data going back to 2017. On the SHFE, the spread between December and January contracts blew out to more than 1,200 yuan a tonne late on Friday, the widest backwardation since 2005.

Chinese smelters are struggling to source concentrate and scrap, and a crackdown on illegal mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo – China’s biggest source of refined copper – in which the government seized more than 500 trucks and several thousand tonnes of copper and cobalt, threatens to crimp supplies further.

“One of the main drivers for the tightness is the slowdown in refined production growth, which reflects the fact that smelters have been struggling for feedstock,” Morgan Stanley metals strategist Amy Gower told Bloomberg. “The demand indicators are fairly lackluster, so it does point to supply issues being the cause of the tightness in the Chinese market.”

Ship to shore

Comex depots hold 732,943 tonnes, more than double a year ago, after two years in which miners and traders prioritised shipments to the US ahead of threatened import tariffs.

On paper, the surge in Shanghai premiums and spreads is now large enough to cover the cost of shipping copper from the US back to China. The hindrance, people familiar with the trade told Bloomberg, is that those cargoes would be worth far more in the US if tariffs are eventually imposed.

“This is starting to become more of a question, but for it to happen I think you’d need tariffs to be definitively ruled out,” Gower said. “Our base case is that the US material will be quite sticky and will only get drawn down through under-importing.”

Temporary gains?

Monday’s bounce may not hold. “Today’s move does not necessarily mark the end of the correction,” ING’s Manthey said. “Prices remain vulnerable to further weakness if broader market sentiment deteriorates again.”

A Democratic sweep in last week’s US midterm elections has reduced the prospects for the Trump administration’s planned tariffs on refined copper and raised the odds of tighter restrictions on data centres, threatening both the AI-related demand and the tariff-driven stockpiling that have supported prices this year. TD Securities said on Friday that copper faces a further slide as the result weakens expectations for import tariffs.

Last week also offered a partial answer to the question of how much of copper’s 2026 rally rests on AI hype rather than fundamentals. Gross says: the metal fell in lockstep with tech stocks. The physical demand story has not changed – US construction spending on data centres hit a record annualized $96.5 billion in September, according to The Copper Journal – but a “not in my backyard” contingent emboldened by the election could see that spending stall too.

Citi struck a similar note on Monday: “While low visible inventories and elevated geopolitical risks should continue to provide downside support in the near-term, the outlook for next year remains challenged by Indonesian-led supply growth and a muted demand environment.”

Miners rebound

Copper producers rallied with the metal on Monday. Freeport-McMoRan climbed 5.8% in early afternoon trade in New York, lifting its market value to $90.2 billion, less than a week after its board approved a $4.5 billion expansion of the Bagdad mine in Arizona that would more than double the operation’s copper output to over 400 million pounds a year from mid-2030 and make it the second-largest copper mine in the US.

Southern Copper added 6.0% to $151.3 billion and Teck Resources rose 5.9% to $31.4 billion. BHP gained 3.2% to $207.4 billion, Rio Tinto 3.0% to $147.8 billion and Glencore 5.3% to $81.7 billion. Anglo American was up 6.2% and Antofagasta 6.7% in US trading, with Lundin Mining up 6.5% and First Quantum Minerals 5.2% in Toronto.

Ivanhoe Mines added 3.5%, but the Vancouver-based company is still down 47% this year after a second production downgrade at its Kamoa-Kakula complex in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The bounce follows a brutal October. The MINING.COM TOP 50 ranking of the world’s most valuable miners lost $226 billion last month on top of September’s $264 billion decline, and is now $712 billion below its February peak.

In project news, Rio Tinto is injecting $144 million into Resolution Copper in Arizona after a land-swap court victory, a project JPMorgan says is central to its view that US copper output could more than double . In Chile, Codelco and Pucobre have cleared a key hurdle for an $870 million copper mine slated to begin construction in 2027, even as the state miner contends with an inflated output scandal that has grown to 42,100 tonnes.
